📖 Worked example — a prompt-engineering rubric aspect, graded

WORKED EXAMPLE — “the submission demonstrates prompt refinement”
Not evident: one prompt, one output, no iteration shown.
Approaching: two prompts, but no explanation of WHY the second is better.
Competent: version 1 → its output → a critique naming the specific failure (too vague / wrong format / missing audience) → version 2 with the targeted fix → improved output → a comparison tying the improvement to the change.

The graded artifact is the LOOP: prompt, output, diagnosis, revision, evidence. Screenshot or transcript each stage — the reasoning between versions carries the points, not the final output alone.

What each rubric aspect is really checking

WGU rubrics for D685 are scored Not Evident / Approaching / Competent per aspect. The stable competencies below are what evaluators look for — the exact aspect numbers and wording change, so verify against your current rubric.

CompetencyWhat evaluators look forHow to nail it
Correct application of named patternsEach required pattern is present, correctly built, and clearly labeled with its verbatim prompt and real outputGive each pattern its own subsection with a heading. Show the prompt in a code block and the output as a screenshot or quoted text. Make sure a few-shot prompt truly has examples and a CoT prompt truly asks for step-by-step reasoning.
Iterative refinement with justificationA v1 prompt, a stated reason it was weak, and a v2 that measurably improves the outputFor at least one (ideally each) pattern, show v1 -> problem -> v2 -> better result. Name the change: added constraints, clarified role, specified format, supplied examples.
Evaluation against criteriaExplicit, named criteria and a judgment of each output against themDefine criteria up front (accuracy, relevance, completeness, tone, format adherence). Rate outputs — a small table or rubric works well — and explain the ratings.
Responsible use / guardrailsConcrete treatment of hallucination, bias, prompt injection, and data privacy tied to your scenarioFor each risk, give a scenario-specific example plus a mitigation (fact-check sources, diverse examples, input sanitization, never pasting PII/secrets).
Clear documentationOrganized, professional, complete, with in-text citations for any sourcesUse consistent headings, label figures, keep prompts/outputs adjacent, and cite tools and sources in APA. Proofread.

The difference between Approaching and Competent

Most returns are not for missing sections but for shallow ones. "I refined the prompt" is Approaching; "v1 hallucinated a statute because it lacked a source constraint, so v2 added 'cite only from the provided text,' which eliminated the fabrication" is Competent. Specificity and cause-effect reasoning move each aspect to Competent.

📖 Worked example — pre-submit sweep for a prompting PA

WORKED EXAMPLE — a returned submission, fixed
Case: returned on “explains the prompt components” — the student submitted excellent prompts but never LABELED which part was persona, context, constraints, or format.
Fix: annotate each prompt: “[persona] You are a… [context] Our team… [format] Output a table…” plus one sentence per component on why it’s there. Resubmit.

The sweep: every required component named AND labeled in your prompts; the refinement loop shown (before/after with reasons); outputs included as evidence (screenshots/transcripts); ethical considerations addressed where the task asks; every task verb matched to a labeled section.

Build it in this order

  1. Lock the scenario. Pick one concrete use case and keep every pattern tied to it for coherence.
  2. List the required patterns. From your current task instructions, confirm which patterns and how many. Create a subsection for each.
  3. Prompt live and capture. Run each pattern in a real LLM. Paste the verbatim prompt and screenshot or copy the exact output. Note the tool and date.
  4. Iterate. For each pattern (or at least several), record v1, why it was weak, v2, and the improved result.
  5. Evaluate. Define criteria (accuracy, relevance, completeness, tone, format) and rate the outputs, ideally in a table.
  6. Address ethics/guardrails. Give scenario-specific hallucination, bias, prompt-injection, and data-privacy examples with mitigations.
  7. Document and cite. Clean headings, labeled figures, APA citations for tools and any sources, then proofread.

Why D685 PAs get returned (avoid these)

  • Patterns named but not demonstrated — no actual prompt/output shown. Include verbatim prompts and real responses for every pattern.
  • No iteration — a single prompt with no v1-to-v2 trail. Always show at least one refinement with justification.
  • No evaluation criteria — subjective "it was good" with no defined standards. State criteria and judge against them.
  • Ethics section missing or generic — vague "AI can be biased" statements. Tie each risk to your scenario with a concrete mitigation.
  • Screenshots/outputs not included — evaluators cannot verify the work. Include or clearly reproduce every output.

Guardrails cheat-sheet

  • Hallucination — the model invents facts/citations. Mitigate: constrain to provided sources, verify claims, ask for citations.
  • Bias — skewed or stereotyped output. Mitigate: diverse few-shot examples, request balanced perspectives, review outputs.
  • Prompt injection — untrusted input overrides instructions. Mitigate: separate/sanitize user input, don't blindly trust pasted content.
  • Data privacy — leaking PII/secrets to a third-party model. Mitigate: never paste sensitive data, use anonymized placeholders, follow org policy.
Before submitting, re-read the actual rubric aspect-by-aspect and confirm each has explicit evidence in your document.

📖 Worked example — a hard prompt-pattern scenario

WORKED EXAMPLE — diagnose and fix a failing prompt
Symptom: “Summarize these 20 support tickets and tell me the top issues” keeps producing vague, inconsistent themes.

Diagnosis: one oversized task, no format contract, no criteria for “top.”
Fix — chain + few-shot + format:
1. Prompt A per ticket: “Extract: product, issue category (one of: billing/bug/how-to), severity 1-3. Output JSON.” (few-shot with 2 labeled tickets pins the categories).
2. Prompt B on the 20 JSON rows: “Aggregate by category, rank by count then severity, output a 5-row table.”
Decomposition made each step verifiable; the format contract made outputs machine-stable; examples pinned the taxonomy. That triple fix is the answer shape for most “why does this prompt fail?” challenges.

Choosing a Pattern by the Shape of the Problem

Prompt patterns are not interchangeable; each solves a specific failure mode. Zero-shot works when the task is common and the model already knows the format. Few-shot is the right tool when you need a specific, hard-to-describe style, structure, or edge-case handling that is easier to show than to state. Chain-of-thought helps multi-step reasoning (math, logic, planning) by asking the model to work through intermediate steps before answering. Persona/role shapes tone, vocabulary, and priorities. Cognitive-verifier makes the model break a question into sub-questions and answer those first. Question-refinement has the model improve your question before answering it. Template/output-format pins the exact structure of the response (JSON keys, columns, headings). ReAct interleaves reasoning with tool calls or actions.

Diagnosing failures

When a prompt fails, match the symptom to the missing pattern. Wrong format (prose instead of JSON) points to a missing template. Wrong content because the task was ambiguous points to under-specification or missing few-shot examples. Arithmetic or logic errors point to a missing chain-of-thought. Confidently wrong facts point to missing grounding, not a new pattern. A good few-shot set is diverse and covers the edge cases you care about, not three near-identical easy examples. Recognizing a pattern in someone else's prompt is the inverse skill: a prompt that says "Let's think step by step" is chain-of-thought; one that gives 3 labeled input/output pairs is few-shot; one that says "Act as a senior tax auditor" is persona.

📖 Worked example — RAG & guardrails, reasoned through

WORKED EXAMPLE — why the chatbot cites last year’s policy
Symptom: an HR chatbot answers vacation questions with outdated numbers.
Cause: the model only “knows” its training data — the new policy postdates its cutoff.
Fix — RAG (retrieval-augmented generation): at question time, SEARCH the current policy docs, paste the relevant passages into the prompt as context, and instruct: “Answer ONLY from the provided documents; if absent, say you don’t know, and cite the section.”

Retrieval supplies fresh knowledge; the grounding instruction is the guardrail against hallucination; the citation requirement makes answers auditable. RAG = search + stuff-the-context + constrain — that trio answers every “how do we make it current/accurate?” question.

Reasoning About the Machine, Not Just the Prompt

Temperature and top-p control randomness in token selection. Low temperature (near 0) makes output deterministic and repeatable, which you want for extraction, classification, and code. High temperature increases diversity, useful for brainstorming and creative variation. Top-p (nucleus sampling) restricts choices to the smallest set of tokens whose probability sums to p; lowering it also narrows variety. The context window is the hard token budget for input plus output combined; exceeding it forces truncation, so long documents must be chunked, summarized, or retrieved rather than pasted wholesale.

Grounding and defense

RAG is the right tool when the model needs current, private, or frequently changing facts it was never trained on; you retrieve relevant passages and put them in context. Fine-tuning teaches durable behavior, format, or style but does not reliably inject fresh facts. Plain prompting handles tasks the base model already knows. To reduce hallucination, ground answers in retrieved sources and instruct the model to say 'I don't know' when the context lacks the answer. Prompt injection is when untrusted content (a web page, a document, user input) contains instructions that try to override your system prompt; defenses include separating trusted from untrusted text, refusing to follow instructions found in data, and output filtering. Match your evaluation metric to the task: exact-match or F1 for extraction, faithfulness/groundedness for RAG, and human or rubric scoring for open-ended generation. System messages set durable rules and role; user messages carry the specific request.

🧠 The Aistote Method (J-Method)

THE IDEA
The Aistote app is built on two of the most evidence-backed study techniques — active recall and spaced repetition — run in short, intense 25-minute blocks (its "J-Method"). Instead of slowly re-reading, you spend the time testing yourself and re-testing what you miss. This app already has every tool the method needs.
THE 3-STEP LOOP
StepWhat you doWhere in this app
1. ConvertTurn the material into questions instead of re-reading it.Open a section, skim the lesson once, then jump to its Quiz.
2. RecallAnswer from memory first — no peeking — then check.Take the section Quiz, or a PA / OA simulation; rate your confidence.
3. Space itRe-test only what you missed, on a growing schedule.Every miss becomes a Flashcard; review them on the app's spaced-repetition schedule.
A 25-MINUTE J-METHOD SESSION
TimeDo this
0–3 minSkim the lesson's key terms and the big idea — don't memorize yet, just get the lay of the land.
3–18 minTake the section quiz (or a 15-question drill). Try to recall the answer first, reveal it after.
18–23 minRedo only the questions you got wrong.
23–25 minSend the stubborn ones to Flashcards and note tomorrow's quick review.
Start the block with the ⚡ Focus timer (25 min) on any lesson — that is your J-Method session.
⚠️ THE ONE RULE
Always try to answer from memory before you look. The effort of retrieving is what actually builds the memory — re-reading feels productive but barely moves it.
WHY IT WORKS
Active recall (testing yourself) forces your brain to reconstruct the answer, which strengthens it far more than recognition. Spaced repetition reviews each fact just as you're about to forget it, moving it into long-term memory with the fewest reps. The 25-minute block simply makes you actually do both, every day.
DAILY RHYTHM
Two or three 25-minute J-Method blocks a day (new material in one, missed-question review in the next) beats a single long cram session — and it's how the Aistote method delivers "learn it in 25 minutes" instead of hours.

Scope and Specificity

Context and Background

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Evaluating Prompt Outputs

⚠ FLUENCY FOOLS PEOPLE Polished prose ≠ correct content — confident wording is exactly how hallucinations slip through. Verification against the source (or an authority) is non-negotiable for factual outputs; that is…

Bias and Fairness

⚠ THE MODEL SAID SO IS NOT A DEFENSE Deploying biased output is the deployer s responsibility — the exam frames this as: bias originates in DATA, surfaces in OUTPUT, and is owned by the HUMAN who uses it.

Privacy, IP, and Misuse

⚠ THE PROMPT IS A DISCLOSURE Anything typed into an external AI service leaves your control. The rule the exam wants: never paste confidential, personal, or regulated data into tools not approved for it.

Responsible AI Use

⚠ AUTOMATION ≠ ABDICATION The recurring exam answer: AI may assist decisions but a HUMAN remains accountable for them — especially consequential ones (hiring, grades, health, credit). The AI decided is never the acceptable justification — a person must be able to explain and own the outcome.

📋 Exam Coverage: RAG & Guardrails

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)

▸ RAG vs FINE-TUNING RAG injects knowledge at query time — best for facts that change, large/private corpora, and citation needs; nothing is retrained. Fine-tuning bakes behavior/style into the model's weights — best for tone, format, and skills, but it's costly and doesn't add fresh facts.

Guardrails: Input/Output Validation & Moderation

▸ PROMPT INJECTION Untrusted text (a user message or a retrieved document) that tries to override the system's instructions. Defenses: treat retrieved/user content as data not commands, keep system instructions authoritative, and validate outputs rather than trusting the model to police itself.
